title: Parameters
jupyter: python3

## Values live in the model

In a declared disease, a value used once lives in the transition that uses it. There is no parameter block to fill in:

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = ss.transmission('S -> I', beta=0.3),
    recovery  = ss.progression('I -> R', dur=ss.days(10)),
    init_prev = 0.01,
)
print(sir.pars)
```

What a number means is given by the slot it is in: `beta=` is a rate, `dur=` is a duration, and `init_prev=` is a fraction of the population. A bare number takes the sim's unit of time (here days, since `ss.days(10)` has a unit), and a typed value such as `ss.perday(0.3)` or `ss.years(5)` keeps its own unit and is converted. See [Time](advanced_time.qmd) for the time types.

## Named parameters: `ss.par`

When a parameter is reused, fitted, or documented, give it a name with `ss.par`. It behaves like its value in arithmetic, so it can be used anywhere a number can:

```{python}
beta = ss.par(0.05, bounds=[0.01, 0.5], source='Made up for this example')
dur  = ss.par(ss.days(10), bounds=[3, 30])

S, I, R = ss.states(3)
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ beta * I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ dur,
    init_prev = 0.01,
)
print(sir.pars)
```

- A named parameter is collected into the module's `pars` under its name (here taken from the variable): `sir.pars.beta`.
- `bounds` is what makes a parameter fittable: `sim.calibrate()` fits every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data (see [Calibration](workflows_calibration.qmd)). A value outside its bounds is an error.
- `source` (where the number came from) and `doc` (what it means) are free text, shown by `describe()`.

Parameter values can also be given to the sim, by name, without changing the model. This is useful for a set of country-specific values or a fitted parameter set:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(sir, pars=dict(beta=0.2), stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0)
sim.run()
print(f'Peak infected: {sim.results.sir.n_I.max():,.0f}')
```

With more than one module, the name is written with the module's, e.g. `pars={'sir.beta': 0.2}`. A name that matches no parameter is an error that lists the parameters there are, so a misspelled parameter is never silently ignored:

```{python}
try:
    ss.Sim(sir, pars=dict(betta=0.2)).init()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'{type(e).__name__}: {e}')
```

## The forms a value can take

Every slot that takes a value accepts every form below; the slot fixes what the value means, and the form is free:

```python
beta = 0.05                                       # a number; unit from the sim
beta = ss.perday(0.05)                            # a typed quantity
beta = ss.lognorm_ex(mean=0.05, std=0.01)         # a distribution: varies between agents
beta = ss.timeseries({'2020-01-01': 0.05, '2021-01-01': 0.02}) # varies in time
beta = ss.seasonal(mean=0.05, amplitude=0.3, peak='January')   # a yearly cycle
beta = ss.by(age=[0.08, 0.05, 0.03])              # one value per stratum (here, per age group)
beta = lambda sim: 0.05 if sim.now < ss.date('2020-03-15') else 0.03 # a function of the sim
```

Any of these can be wrapped in `ss.par(...)` to give it a name, bounds, or a source. For example, here transmission falls on a date, given as a time series and as a function of the sim, which give the same answer:

```{python}
def make_sir(beta):
    return ss.Disease(
        infection = ss.transmission('S -> I', beta=beta),
        recovery  = ss.progression('I -> R', dur=ss.days(10)),
        init_prev = 0.01,
        name = 'sir',
    )

betas = dict(
    constant   = 0.3,
    timeseries = ss.timeseries({'2020-01-01': 0.3, '2020-01-20': 0.1}),
    function   = lambda sim: 0.3 if sim.now < ss.date('2020-01-20') else 0.1,
)
for label, beta in betas.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(make_sir(beta), start='2020-01-01', stop='2020-07-01', verbose=0).run()
    print(f'{label:10s} total infected: {sim.results.sir.n_R[-1]:,.0f}')
```

A distribution means two different things depending on where it is put. As a value (`dur=ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(10), std=ss.days(3))`) it gives each agent their own value. As a prior (`ss.par(0.05, prior=ss.lognorm_ex(mean=0.05, std=0.01))`) it is uncertainty about one number, used only by calibration. A compartmental run has no individuals to draw for, so a dwell-time distribution is run as Erlang sub-stages (with a note), and a distribution on anything else, such as `beta`, makes the model run as agents.

## Parameters that depend on the agent

A function given to a slot can also take the agents it is asked about, `fn(sim, uids)`, and return one value per agent. For example, in reality the duration of infection of a disease might vary by age. We could model this as follows, with the duration in years equal to a tenth of the person's age:

```{python}
import sciris as sc
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = ss.transmission('S -> I', beta=ss.peryear(0.5)),
    recovery  = ss.progression('I -> R', dur=lambda sim, uids: ss.years(sim.people.age[uids] / 10)),
    init_prev = 0.05,
)
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=20e3, start='2000', stop='2010', diseases=sir, networks='random')
sim.run()
sim.plot()

# Show the age distribution of infections
ages = sim.people.age[:]
infected_ages = ages[sim.diseases.sir.I]

fig = plt.figure()

plt.subplot(2,1,1)
plt.hist(ages, bins=range(0,100,5))
plt.title('Simulation age distribution')
plt.xlabel('Age')
plt.ylabel('Number of people')

plt.subplot(2,1,2)
plt.hist(infected_ages, bins=range(0,100,5))
plt.title('Infection age distribution')
plt.xlabel('Age')
plt.ylabel('Number of people')

sc.figlayout()
plt.show()
```

A function that uses `uids` or a per-agent attribute such as age needs agents, so this sim runs as agents (here it would anyway, because of the network). Using similar logic, any other parameter could be set to depend on anything that the sim is aware of, including time or agent properties like age, sex, or health attributes.

## Parameters of modules written as code

When you write a module as code (for example a disease that subclasses `ss.Infection`), you define the default format of its parameters with `self.define_pars()`:

```{python}
class MySIR(ss.Infection):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            beta = ss.peryear(0.1),
            init_prev = ss.bernoulli(p=0.01),
            dur_inf = ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(6)),
            p_death = ss.bernoulli(p=0.01),
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)

        self.define_states(
            ss.BoolState('susceptible', default=True, label='Susceptible'),
            ss.BoolState('infected', label='Infectious'),
            ss.BoolState('recovered', label='Recovered'),
            ss.FloatArr('ti_infected', label='Time of infection'),
            ss.FloatArr('ti_recovered', label='Time of recovery'),
            ss.FloatArr('ti_dead', label='Time of death'),
            ss.FloatArr('rel_sus', default=1.0, label='Relative susceptibility'),
            ss.FloatArr('rel_trans', default=1.0, label='Relative transmission'),
            reset = True, # Do not use any existing states
        )
        return
```

The point of `self.define_pars()` is to set the ground truth for the format that the parameters should take. When users enter their own parameters for defining an instance of this module, the parameter values they enter will be processed within `self.update_pars()` and will be checked for consistency with the format provided in the original parameters (`define_pars`). For example, the parameter `p_death` in the example above is specified initially as a Bernoulli distribution. It would be perfectly legitimate to create an instance of the module using any of the following formats:

```{python}
sir1 = MySIR(p_death=0.02)
sir2 = MySIR(p_death=ss.bernoulli(p=0.2))
```

However, it would NOT be ok to create it with e.g. `MySIR(p_death=ss.lognorm_ex(4))`, because if a distribution is defined as a Bernoulli in `define_pars()`, it can't be changed. This is only the case for Bernoulli distributions; other distributions can be changed, e.g. `MySIR(dur_inf=ss.normal(4))` would be okay. This is because Bernoulli distributions have different methods than other distributions, e.g. a `filter()` method that returns `True` for agents which pass the filter.

In a module written as code, a distribution's parameters can themselves be functions, which take the module, the sim, and the agents: `ss.normal(loc=lambda self, sim, uids: sim.people.age[uids] / 10)` gives a duration that depends on age, as in the declared example above. See [Distributions](advanced_distributions.qmd) for more.
